question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

2.text:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented, so the 9 U stickers are all the
same colour and carry no information.  What is left to recognise is the
permutation of the 4 U layer edges and the 4 U layer corners.

On the U layer you have

* 4 U edges : 1 side sticker per edge,
* 4 U corners : 2 side stickers per corner,

i.e. $4\times 1+4\times 2=12$ non-U stickers on the U layer.  That is the
whole amount of side information that the U layer can ever show you from
above.  In practice you never need the whole set.

One side sticker is enough to identify an edge and one side sticker is
enough to identify a corner up to the well known U-layer parity, so the
recognisable data is the 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers,
8 distinct U-layer pieces.  Counting both stickers of a corner the
information is contained in the 12 side stickers of the U layer.  The
information theoretic minimum is much smaller – $\log _{2}21\approx
4.4$ bit – and in normal speed recognition the 21 PLL classes can in fact
be distinguished with 4–6 well chosen side stickers, the conventional
textbook description being the 4 edge stickers together with the 4
corner stickers, i.e. the 8 pieces / 12 stickers of the U layer.  This is
the amount of non-U information that has to be available for a
complete, unambiguous PLL identification.

3.text:
In CFOP the last layer is first oriented. After OLL the U face is
monochrome, so the U face itself gives you no information at all about
the permutation. What is left to be distinguished is the relative
ordering of the 8 U–slice pieces

* 4 U edges – 1 side sticker per edge, 4 stickers
* 4 U corners – 2 side stickers per corner, 8 stickers

i.e. 12 side stickers belong to the U slice.  Up to a horizontal
rotation the 21 PLL classes are distinguished by the side colours of
the 8 pieces.  In particular the edge permutation is given by the four
U–edge side stickers UF, UR, UB, UL and the corner permutation is given
by one side colour per U corner.  That is the 4 + 4 = 8 distinct
side-colours that a cuber actually looks at in practice.  Of course the
U slice carries 4×1+4×2 = 12 non-U stickers in total and the 12 stickers
together completely specify the U–slice permutation, the 8th sticker
being parity redundant.  This is the usual “you never look at the U
face, you look at the side colours of the U layer’’ statement.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d count 9. After OLL, the top face is uniform, so PLL must be read from the side stickers of the last layer. Looking at only two adjacent sides gives 6 stickers, but that can leave ambiguous cases where the corner/edge cycles look like a rotated version of another PLL, especially with symmetric cases like H, N, or G perms. To pin down the exact PLL without relying on AUF or a memorized two-sided signature, you need to see three sides of the last layer: 3 stickers per side × 3 sides = 9 non-top-facing stickers. The fourth side is then forced by elimination.

8.text:
In CFOP the U layer is OLL solved so that the nine U stickers are all the
same colour and carry no information at all.  What is left to be decided
is the permutation of the four U corners and the four U edges.

The U layer has

* 4 U edges.  An U edge is completely identified by the one side sticker
which is not on U, 4 stickers;
* 4 U corners.  A U corner is completely identified by the two side
stickers which are not on U, 2 stickers per corner.

Hence the U layer carries 4+2·4 = 12 side stickers and it is those 12
side stickers which carry the whole PLL information.  In an absolute
sense you have to know the colour pattern of the whole 12-sticker
ring in order to know the permutation of the eight U pieces.  That is
the 12 non-U stickers of the U layer, 8 corner side stickers and 4 edge
side stickers.

In a normal head on view you never see the whole ring at once.  Up to a
rotation about the U axis the ring is completely determined by the six
side stickers that are visible on the front and right top rows, i.e. the
three front top stickers UF–UFR and the three right top stickers UFR–UBR.
Modulo the four U rotations this six sticker view is information
theoretically more than enough to separate the 21 PLL classes, and it is
the view that is used in practice.  With a little redundancy the 21
classes can be separated with 7–8 distinct side stickers, the six-sticker
front/right view being the conventional practical minimum.  This is the
12-sticker U ring quoted above.

6.text:
In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face monochrome.  The U face itself is
therefore information free for the permutation step and the whole of the
PLL information is carried by the side colours of the U-slice.

The U-slice contains

* 4 U-edges.  After the OLL each U-edge is identified by the single
side colour that it shows on F/R/B/L.  4 stickers.
* 4 U-corners.  After the OLL each U-corner is identified by the two
side colours that it shows on F/R/B/L.  2×4 = 8 stickers.

Hence the U-slice has

4 + 8 = 12

non-U stickers, viz. the 12 side stickers of the 4 U-edges and the 4
U-corners.  Seeing the whole U-slice is a complete invariant for the
U-permutation and therefore for the 21 PLL classes.  In practice the
12 stickers are highly redundant and a PLL can be narrowed down in the
normal speed-cubing sense with the familiar headlights / bar / etc.
information, i.e. with the 4 U-edge side stickers and a few of the
U-corner side stickers, typically 6–8 stickers in the worst case, the
information-theoretic lower bound being  log5 21 ≈ 2 stickers.  The
12 side stickers of the U-slice are the set which is normally quoted as
the U-layer PLL information. ∎

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 5 — After OLL, the top face is uniform, so PLL recognition depends only on the side stickers around the last layer. A common two-side inspection shows six stickers, but one of them is redundant: the corner at the intersection of the two viewed faces has two side stickers, and once the other five stickers are visible, the sixth is forced by the known top color and last-layer permutation parity. Thus the minimum number of non-top-facing stickers needed to distinguish all 21 PLL cases is five.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 5. After OLL, the top face is uniform, so PLL recognition depends only on the side stickers. The usual “two-sided” view shows six stickers, but the sixth is redundant: if you take all three stickers on one side and the edge sticker plus the far-corner sticker on an adjacent side, the shared corner’s second sticker is forced by the corner piece already visible and the color-count/parity constraints. Those five non-top-facing stickers determine the permutation of the last-layer edges and corners, so they are enough to distinguish all 21 PLL cases. Six is just a convenient convention, not the minimum.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8. After OLL, the top face is uniform, so the PLL is encoded in the side stickers of the last-layer pieces. There are four last-layer edges, each with one non-top sticker, and four last-layer corners. For a corner, seeing just one of its two side stickers is enough to identify the piece, since the top sticker is already oriented up and the other side color is fixed by the color scheme. To fully identify the PLL, you need to know the permutation of all eight last-layer pieces, so you need at least one side sticker from each of the eight cubies: 4 edges + 4 corners = 8. Fewer stickers can sometimes narrow it down, but they do not guarantee distinguishing every PLL case without relying on inference or elimination.

10.text:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented by the OLL so that the whole U face
is the same colour.  The only thing that is left to recognise is the
permutation of the 8 U pieces

* 4 U edges : each U edge is identified on the side by the one side
sticker which is not on U,
* 4 U corners : each U corner is identified on the side by the two side
stickers which are not on U.

In particular a U edge is known as soon as you see its one side sticker
and a U corner is known as soon as you see one of its two side stickers,
the second side sticker being fixed by the known orientation of the
corner.  Hence in practice PLL recognition is the recognition of

* the four U-edge side stickers, 1 per edge, and
* one side sticker per U-corner,

i.e. the eight distinct side stickers of the U layer.  The U layer has in
all

4·1 + 4·2 = 12

non-U stickers.  Because the permutation of the U edges and the
permutation of the U corners have the same parity the 8th piece is
implied by the other seven, so seven independent non-U observations are
in principle enough to fix the 21 PLL classes.  This is normally quoted
as the eight side stickers of the U layer, four edges and four corners,
12 stickers in all on the U layer, seven of which are independent.  The
12 stickers are the 4 edge side stickers + the 8 corner side stickers
that are usually spoken of as the 8 side stickers that are looked at in
practice.

11.text:
In CFOP the U face is already solved so the 9 U stickers carry no
information.  What is left to tell is the permutation of the 8 pieces
that sit on the U layer.  Up to a rotation of the cube an edge is
identified by the single side sticker that it shows on the side of the
cube and a corner is identified by the two side stickers that it shows
on the side of the cube.  On the U layer there are

* 4 U–edges, 1 side sticker each, 4 stickers, and
* 4 U–corners, 2 side stickers each, 8 stickers,

i.e. 12 non-U sticker faces in total on the U layer.  Up to rotation
the permutation of the four edges is fixed by the four edge side
stickers and the permutation of the four corners is fixed by one
distinguishing side sticker per corner.  In ordinary recognition that
is the eight distinct side stickers that are normally quoted,

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct
non-U stickers,

the four corner side stickers being the four that are visible on the
side of the cube you are looking at.  The full unambiguous
U-layer description is the 12 side faces 4×1+4×2 of the U layer, the
fourth edge and the second side of each corner being parity
determined by the first.  This is why PLL is normally said to be a
purely U-layer recognition: no D-layer sticker is ever needed.

4.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome.  The 9 U stickers are all the same
colour and carry no information about the permutation that is left to do.
All of the information that distinguishes one PLL from another is carried
by the side stickers of the U–layer.

The U–layer has

* 4 U–edges, each with one side sticker, 4 stickers
* 4 U–corners, each with two side stickers, 8 stickers

i.e. 12 non–U stickers in total.  Up to rotation the 21 PLLs are
distinguished by the cyclic order of the four edge side colours and the
cyclic order of the four corner side colours.  In information theoretic
terms 4–6 of those side stickers already carry 21 possibilities and in
practice the recognition is taught as the 4 edge side stickers together
with one identifiable side sticker per corner, 8 distinct non–U stickers,
the 12 stickers of the U ring being the information that is actually
visible.  That is the 6–8 sticker recognition that is normally quoted,
the 4 edge + 4 corner = 8 sticker, i.e. the 12 sticker U ring, version of
it.  In the usual two face view this is the familiar 6 sticker
front/back top row view, which is the minimal sufficient set that is
used in practice.

12.text:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented after OLL so the nine U stickers
are all the same colour and carry no permutation information at all.
The permutation of the last layer is the permutation of the eight
U-layer cubies

* 4 U edges – each edge is U + one side colour.  The U colour is known
so the side colour alone identifies the edge piece.  One side sticker
per edge is therefore enough and the four edge side stickers are
UFR–UFL–UBL–UBR.
* 4 U corners – each corner is U + two side colours.  The U colour is
known so the identity of the corner is fixed by the unordered pair of
side colours.  In practice one side sticker per corner is enough to
read the relative order of the four corners, the second side sticker
being then forced by the position.

Hence in the information theoretic sense you have to read one side
sticker for each of the eight U-layer pieces, i.e. eight non-U stickers.
The U-layer in total carries

* 4 edges × 1 side sticker = 4
* 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 8

12 non-top stickers.  From a fixed viewing position you can see the
whole U-row of two adjacent side faces, i.e. three stickers on the
Front U-row and three stickers on the Right U-row, six distinct
non-U stickers of the U-layer at once.  A U turn brings the other two
edge side stickers and the other two corner side stickers into view,
so that the eight distinct piece-identifying side stickers, the four
edge side stickers and four corner side stickers, are the information
that is actually used for PLL recognition.  This is the twelve
non-top stickers of the U-layer, eight of which are distinct piece
identifiers, six of which are visible simultaneously.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d say 7. After OLL, the top face is uniform, so the PLL information is carried by the side stickers of the last layer. The usual two-sided PLL recognition uses the three stickers on each of two adjacent faces, which is 6 stickers. However, that is only enough to narrow the case down to a family; because the U layer can be rotated, some PLLs (notably the G-perms and the R-perms) can share the same two-side signature until you see one additional sticker from a third side. That extra sticker breaks the remaining AUF/symmetry ambiguity, so you need 7 non-top-facing stickers to fully identify the PLL case.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The U face is monochrome after OLL so all PLL information is in the side stickers of the U-layer.

* U-layer inventory: 4 U-edges ×1 side sticker =4, 4 U-corners ×2 side stickers =8. 4+8=12 non-U stickers in total on the U-layer. This is the complete U-ring that carries the permutation.
* Piece identification: an edge is identified by its single side colour, a corner by its unordered pair of side colours. With the U colour known one side sticker per corner is enough in practice to read the relative order, giving the usual “4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct piece-identifying stickers’’ that cubers quote. The 12 stickers are redundant by parity: the permutation of edges and corners have the same parity, so the 8th piece is implied and 7 independent non-U observations are information-theoretically enough to fix the 21 PLL classes.

Current disagreement in the round:
- 12 total non-U stickers on the U-layer is the full description, 8 distinct identifiers in normal use.
- Practical viewing: from a fixed head-on view the front+right top rows give 6 stickers at once; a U turn brings the rest into view.
- Minimalist claims: 7 independent stickers due to parity, 5-6 stickers claimed sufficient for the 21 classes with AUF/symmetry exploitation, 9 stickers claimed if three sides are insisted on.

Unresolved: whether the question asks for the total information content of the U-layer, 12, the conventional 8 piece-identifying stickers, or the information-theoretic minimum ~7 and the commonly quoted practical minimum 6. The consensus description in the literature is the 12 side stickers of the U-layer, normally used as 8 distinct side stickers.

U-layer inventory:

information is carried by the side stickers of the U slice.

The U slice is

* 4 U edges : 1 side sticker per edge, 4 stickers UF, UR, UB, UL
* 4 U corners : 2 side stickers per corner, 2×4 = 8 stickers

i.e. 4+8 = 12 non-U stickers in total on the U layer.  That 12-sticker
U-ring is the complete invariant for the U-permutation and hence for the
21 PLL classes. No D-layer sticker is ever needed.

Up to a U rotation an edge is identified by its single side colour and a
corner is identified by the unordered pair of its two side colours. The
U colour is already known from OLL so one side colour per corner is enough
to read the relative order of the four corners, the second side colour
being forced by the piece and the orientation.  In the piece-identifying
sense the data that is actually used is therefore

* 4 edge side stickers, one per U edge, and
* 1 side sticker per U corner

4 + 4 = 8 distinct non-U stickers, the 12 physical side stickers of the U
ring.  Because the U edge permutation and the U corner permutation have
the same parity the 8th piece is parity implied by the other seven, so
seven independent non-U observations are information theoretically
enough to fix the 21 PLL classes.  The familiar two-face inspection is the
six sticker front-top + right-top view of that eight-sticker set, the
remaining two stickers being brought in by a U/AUF.

That is the usual statement that PLL is a purely U-layer recognition:
12 side stickers on the U layer, 8 distinct piece-identifying non-U
stickers, 7 independent.  In the textbook 8-sticker counting this is
often quoted simply as the 8 side stickers of the U layer, 4 edges + 4
corners, i.e. the 12-sticker U ring.

10.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome. The nine U stickers are then
information free for the permutation step and the whole of the PLL
information is carried by the side stickers of the U-slice.

The U-slice is

* 4 U-edges.  After OLL an U-edge is U + one side colour. The U colour
is known so the edge piece is identified by its single side sticker.
4 × 1 = 4 non-U stickers;
* 4 U-corners.  After OLL an U-corner is U + two side colours. The U
colour and the corner orientation are known so the corner piece is
identified by the unordered pair of its two side colours. 2 × 4 = 8
non-U stickers.

Hence the U-slice carries

4·1 + 4·2 = 12

non-top stickers in total, 4 edge side stickers and 8 corner side
stickers.  That is the complete U-layer invariant for the permutation.

In the usual piece-identifying sense one side sticker per cubie is enough:
one side sticker identifies a U-edge and one side sticker is enough to
identify a U-corner once the U orientation is known.  That is the
normally quoted

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8

distinct non-U piece identifiers, the 12 stickers of the U-ring being the
full 4+8 description.  Up to the edge-corner parity the 8th piece is
implied by the other seven, and up to a U rotation the familiar two-face
top-row view shows six distinct non-U stickers at once, a U turn
bringing the rest of the 8 distinct identifiers into view.  This is the
12-sticker, 8-distinct-sticker U-layer PLL information that is normally
quoted as “the PLL is a purely U-layer recognition”.

8.text:
In CFOP the OLL leaves the U face monochrome. The 9 U stickers therefore carry
no permutation information at all and the whole PLL information lives in the
U–slice.

The U–slice is

* 4 U–edges : 1 side sticker per edge, 4 stickers
* 4 U–corners : 2 side stickers per corner, 8 stickers

4·1 + 4·2 = 12 non–U stickers on the U layer. That 12-sticker U-ring is a
complete invariant for the U permutation and hence for the 21 PLL classes
up to AUF.

The redundancy is well known. The U colour is known so an U-edge is identified
by its single side colour and an U-corner is identified by the unordered pair
of its two side colours. In recognitional terms that is

4 edge side stickers + 1 side sticker per corner = 8 distinct piece–identifying
non-U stickers,

the 12 stickers being the 4 edge side stickers + the 8 corner side stickers.

the 8th piece is parity implied, so 7 independent non-U observations are
information-theoretically enough to fix the 21 classes up to U rotation.

11.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome, the nine U stickers carry no
permutation information.  The whole of the PLL information is therefore
carried by the side stickers of the U-slice.

6.text:
In CFOP the OLL leaves the U face monochrome.  The nine U stickers are then
information free for permutation and the whole of the PLL information is
carried by the side colours of the U slice.

* 4 U edges : 1 side sticker per edge  → 4 stickers

In recognition the U colour is known, so an U edge is identified by its
single side sticker and an U corner is identified up to the known U
orientation by one of its two side stickers.  Hence the piece
identifying data is

* 4 edge side stickers, one per U edge, and
* 1 side sticker per U corner,

are the four that are visible on the side you are looking at.  The 8th

permutation have the same parity – so seven independent non-U

complete side information of the last layer.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still think 8 is the cleanest answer if we take “must be seen” literally. After OLL, the U face is uniform, so the PLL is just the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces. Each edge is identified by its single side sticker; each corner is identified by one of its side stickers, because the U sticker is already up and the other side sticker is forced by the piece’s orientation in that position. That means there are four edge side stickers and four corner side stickers—one per piece—that directly tell you which piece is where. The familiar two-sided six-sticker view is a recognition shortcut: it only directly covers five of the eight pieces, and the rest are inferred from parity/color-scheme constraints. If the question were “how few stickers can a trained solver use to infer the PLL?”, 6 would be the usual practical answer. But the wording here is “must be seen to fully identify,” so I’d count the eight distinct piece-identifying stickers. 5 and 7 either drop a piece or rely on parity, and 9 is overkill because the fourth side is forced. So I’d keep 8.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the cleanest way to settle this is to distinguish the *practical two-sided glance* from the number of non-top stickers that actually have to be observed to identify the PLL without relying on an implicit AUF/parity shortcut.

After OLL, the U face is monochrome, so the PLL information is entirely in the side stickers of the last layer. The PLL is the permutation of the 8 U-layer pieces. To identify that permutation directly:

- Each U-layer edge is identified by its one non-top side sticker: 4 edge stickers.
- Each U-layer corner is identified by one side sticker once its position is known, because the U sticker is already on top and the other side color is forced by the corner piece and color scheme: 4 corner stickers.

That gives 4 + 4 = 8 distinct piece-identifying non-top stickers. The full U-layer ring has 12 side stickers, but the extra corner side stickers are redundant once you have one identifying sticker per corner.

The 6-sticker two-face view is a very useful speed-recognition convention, but it works by matching against known PLL signatures and using parity/AUF constraints. If the question is how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case, the natural minimal observed set is one per U-layer piece: 8. I’d go with 8.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still favoring **8** as the literal “must be seen” count. The key issue is that **6** is a trained recognition shortcut, not the number of non-top stickers that directly identify every U-layer piece.

After OLL, the U face is uniform, so the PLL is determined by the side stickers of the eight U-layer pieces: four edges and four corners. Each U-layer edge needs its single side sticker to be identified, and each U-layer corner can be identified by one side sticker because the U sticker is already on top and the corner’s other side color is forced by the piece/orientation. That’s **4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 piece-identifying stickers**.

The familiar two-sided 6-sticker view is real and practical, but it works because you’re matching learned PLL signatures and using AUF/parity/color-scheme constraints. It doesn’t literally show one identifying side sticker for each of the eight U-layer pieces; in the standard F/R top-row view, the shared UFR corner is seen twice while other pieces are inferred. So 6 is enough to *recognize* the PLL case quickly, but it is not the number of non-top stickers that must be directly seen to fully identify the permutation under the wording of the question.

Seven also depends on parity inference, and 12 is the full U-ring rather than the minimal piece-identifying set. If we are counting what must actually be observed, **8** remains the cleanest answer.

3.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. 
PLL is the permutation of the 8 U-layer cubies and is therefore contained
entirely in the side information of the U-slice.

Physically the U-slice has

* 4 U-edges : 1 side sticker per edge = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners : 2 side stickers per corner = 8 non-U stickers

4+8 = 12 non-U stickers on the U-ring. That 12 sticker ring is the complete
physical invariant for the U permutation and for the 21 PLL classes, and
no D-layer sticker is ever needed.

In piece-identifying terms the U colour is known, so

* an U-edge is identified by its single side colour,
* an U-corner is identified by the unordered pair of its two side colours,
  with the U colour known the orientation is known and one side sticker
  per corner is enough to read which corner is where, the second side
  colour being forced by the colour scheme.

Hence the recognitional data that is actually used is

4 edge side stickers + 1 side sticker per corner = 4 + 4 = 8
distinct non-U piece identifiers.

The 12 physical side stickers are 4 edge + 8 corner, i.e. the 8
identifiers plus the second side of each corner. Edge parity = corner
parity makes the 8th piece parity implied, so 7 independent non-U
observations are information theoretically enough, and the familiar
speed view is the 6 sticker front U-row + right U-row view which with
AUF gives access to the 8 distinct identifiers. The clean literal
“one identifier per U-layer piece’’ count is the 8 distinct non-U stickers,
the 12 sticker U-ring being the full physical description.

8.text:
After OLL the U face is information free for permutation.

The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies.

* 4 U-corners: each is U + two side colours. The U colour and the orientation are known after OLL, so the corner piece is identified by the unordered pair of its two side colours. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U piece identifiers.
